explanations.explanation: That's what verse 1 says, friend. His disciples were hungry, so they began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. It's like sneaking a cookie off the cooling rack while you walk past. Hold onto that snack, because somebody is about to have a LOT to say about it.

Not this time, friend. Verse 1 says the disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. So the picking and the eating both happened, right there in the grainfield. Hungry people plus a field full of grain, and the story takes off from there.

explanations.answer: They're doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. The Pharisees, a group of religious leaders, say, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.” They look at a few hungry people picking grain and see a rule being broken. I think they stared so hard at the rulebook that they forgot to look at the people holding the grain.

explanations.answer: They're picking from somebody else's field
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, but the Pharisees never mention whose field it is. Their complaint is about the day. They say the disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:2). Nothing in the text points to a property line.

explanations.answer: They're eating without washing their hands
explanations.explanation: Hand washing is a real complaint, and the Pharisees do bring it up in Matthew 15:2. But it isn't the complaint in this field. Here they say the disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath. Different day, same crowd with a lot of opinions.

Yes, friend. Jesus says David entered the house of God. David, Israel's king, went in with his hungry companions and they ate the consecrated bread. Jesus pulls an example out of Scripture instead of arguing. I think that's a clever way to answer people who say they know the rules.

Adullam is a real cave in David's story (1 Samuel 22:1), so nice memory, friend. But it isn't the place Jesus names here. He says David entered the house of God. That's where the consecrated bread was.

David was a king, so a palace sounds reasonable, friend. But Jesus never says palace. He says David entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread there. No palace in this story.

That's it, friend. Jesus says the consecrated bread was not lawful for David and his companions to eat, but only for the priests. And they ate it anyway. Jesus uses that moment from Scripture to answer the Pharisees.

Elders is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says the consecrated bread was lawful only for the priests. It was not lawful for David and his companions. So the priests are the ones the bread was set aside for.

Prophets are all over the Bible, so I get the guess, friend. But in this verse Jesus says the consecrated bread was for the priests only. David and his companions ate bread that was not lawful for them. Priests are the word to remember.

Careful, friend, because Jesus says the opposite. He says the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent (Matthew 12:5). He asks if the Pharisees haven't read that in the Law. So the word is innocent, not guilty.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “…the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent?” He points to the Law itself for this. The Pharisees were the ones handing out accusations, and Jesus hands them a verse about innocent priests.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here.” He just talked about the priests serving in the temple, and now He says there's One greater. That is a big claim, and He says it plainly.

explanations.answer: A priest sent from the temple
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend, since priests were just in the conversation. But Jesus doesn't say a priest is here. He says One greater than the temple is here. A priest from the temple wouldn't be greater than the temple.

That sounds reasonable, friend, but Jesus says no such thing. He says, “But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here.” Notice He says One, not a message. He's talking about someone who is here.

You got it, friend. Jesus says, “If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent.” He uses the word innocent for the ones the Pharisees had condemned. It's the same word He used about the priests a moment earlier.

The poor are close to God's heart all through the Bible, friend, so I see the guess. But Jesus says the Pharisees would not have condemned the innocent. That's the word in verse 7. The Pharisees had condemned people who were innocent.

Strangers is a thoughtful guess, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says that if they'd known the meaning of “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” they would not have condemned the innocent. This was about the people they had just accused in the grainfield. Innocent is the word to hold onto.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” Son of Man is a name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). The Pharisees brought up the Sabbath, and Jesus finishes by saying who is Lord of it.
A field full of grain makes harvest feel right, friend. But Jesus says Lord of the Sabbath. The Sabbath is the day the Pharisees were arguing about. Harvest is a good word, just not this verse.

Vineyards show up in plenty of Jesus' teachings, friend, so I see where that came from. But this scene is a grainfield, and the line is about the Sabbath. Jesus says the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath. No grapes were harmed in this passage.

That's right, friend. Verse 10 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him…” So the question wasn't curiosity. It had a hook in it, like an ad that says FREE in giant letters and the fine print runs a full page.

Honor would be a nicer reason, friend, but verse 10 doesn't say that. It says they asked in order to accuse Jesus. The man with the withered hand was right there while they asked. The text names accusing as the reason.

I see why you picked it, friend, since people were following Jesus around. But verse 10 says they asked Him in order to accuse Him. That's the word in the text. Following is not what they had in mind with this question.

explanations.answer: Take hold of it and lift it out
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus asks, “…will he not take hold of it and lift it out?” Nobody stands at the edge of a pit checking the calendar first. Jesus uses that picture to show what the Pharisees already do themselves.

explanations.answer: Leave it there until the Sabbath ends
explanations.explanation: That's what the Pharisees' rule might make you think, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says. He asks if the owner will not take hold of the sheep and lift it out. Jesus expects the owner to rescue it on the Sabbath. The sheep doesn't wait for the day to end.

explanations.answer: Ask a priest whether he can help
explanations.explanation: Asking a priest is a careful idea, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention a priest anywhere in this picture. He says the owner will take hold of the sheep and lift it out. The man does it himself. There's no committee meeting at the pit.
That's the word, friend. Jesus says, “How much more valuable is a man than a sheep!” He just talked about lifting a sheep out of a pit. Then He says a man is worth much more than that.
Careful is a good quality, friend, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “How much more valuable is a man than a sheep!” He is comparing worth. A man is worth much more than a sheep.
Patience is a fine thing to have, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Jesus says a man is much more valuable than a sheep. He's comparing what each one is worth. Valuable is the word to remember.
Yes, friend. Jesus says, “Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” He says it right after the sheep in the pit and the value of a man. That's His answer to the question about healing.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says, “Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” He says it right after pointing out that a man is more valuable than a sheep. So He says yes to doing good on the Sabbath.

Yes, friend. Jesus says to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” That's all He says, and the man does it. I'd love to know how it felt to stretch out that hand, but the text doesn't say, so I'll just guess it was something.

explanations.answer: Go and wash in the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's another healing story, friend. Naaman, an army commander from Aram, was told to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10). But Jesus doesn't send this man anywhere. He tells the man, “Stretch out your hand.”

explanations.answer: Go show yourself to the priest
explanations.explanation: That line is real, friend, but it's from another healing. Jesus tells a man with leprosy to show himself to the priest (Matthew 8:4). Here He sends the man nowhere. He says, “Stretch out your hand.”
Careful, friend, because the text says more than that. Verse 13 says the hand was restored to full use, just like the other. Not a little better and not mostly. All the way.
You got it, friend. The man stretched out his hand and it was restored to full use, just like the other. So it wasn't a half fix. The whole thing was made right, all in one moment.

That's what verse 14 says, friend. The Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus. A man just got his hand restored, and this is how they responded. I think this part is heavy, so we'll let it be heavy.

I wish that were the answer, friend, but verse 14 says the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus. A man's hand had just been restored. This part of the story is heavy, and it's okay to feel that.
That's right, friend. Verse 15 says, “Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place.” He knew about the plot and He left. The text doesn't give a reason beyond that, so I'll leave it at that.

explanations.answer: He goes back into their synagogue
explanations.explanation: Jesus did go into their synagogue earlier, friend, but not this time. Verse 15 says He withdrew from that place. So He left instead of going back in. That's the move in the text.

explanations.answer: He sends His disciples to them
explanations.explanation: That's an interesting idea, friend, but the text doesn't say it. Verse 15 says Jesus withdrew from that place. No messengers are mentioned. He is the one who moves.
Yes, friend. Verse 15 says large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all. Not some of them. All of them, and the crowds were large.
Not quite, friend. Verse 15 says large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all. That's every one of them, from a crowd that was large. Nobody is left out in that sentence.
That's right, friend. Verse 16 says He healed them all, “warning them not to make Him known.” The text doesn't give His reason in that verse. Matthew moves right on to the words of Isaiah.

explanations.answer: Not to follow Him any farther
explanations.explanation: The crowds were following Him, so I can see that guess, friend. But the warning in verse 16 isn't about following. He warns them not to make Him known. Following isn't what He tells them to stop.

explanations.answer: Not to go back to the synagogue
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, since the synagogue was where the trouble started. But verse 16 doesn't say anything about the synagogue. It says He warned the crowds not to make Him known. That's the warning.

Careful, friend, because it's the reverse. The words from Isaiah say, “He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.” So no quarreling and no crying out. No voice carrying down the street.

You got it, friend. The words from Isaiah, the prophet, say, “He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.” So the Servant doesn't quarrel and doesn't cry out. A very different kind of loud from the one I use at my ovens.

explanations.answer: He will not break or extinguish them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The words say, “A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish…” Most of us would snuff out a wick that's barely glowing. These words say the Servant won't.

explanations.answer: He will gather and burn them
explanations.explanation: I see where you went, friend, but that's the opposite of the words. The words say a bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish. Nothing in those lines gathers or burns. The Servant leaves them be.

explanations.answer: He will cut and replace them
explanations.explanation: Cut and replace would be the tidy move, friend, but it isn't in the words from Isaiah. They say, “A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish…” So no cutting and no snuffing out. Nothing gets swapped.
That's right, friend. The last line says, “In His name the nations will put their hope.” That's how Matthew closes the words from Isaiah. The nations put their hope in His name.

Fear would be a heavy way to end, friend, but that isn't the word. The last line says the nations will put their hope in His name. Hope is the word in verse 21. The words from Isaiah end on a note of hope.

Doubt is a fair human guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, “In His name the nations will put their hope.” Hope is the word the passage closes on. That's the last word before the next part of Matthew.
